questions.text: ANA: Which of the following cells is not a neuroglia?
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are large neurons of the cerebellar cortex, not glial cells. Astrocytes, ependymal cells, oligodendrocytes and microglia are all neuroglia of the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cells are neurons, not neuroglia.

questions.text: Locate the site of Somatosensory Area 1 (S1) and describe its body representation. (3 Marks)
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) occupies the postcentral gyrus and processes contralateral discriminative touch, proprioception and conscious sensation. Its body map is an inverted homunculus, with the leg on the medial surface and the face most laterally. Areas with high receptor density, such as the hand and face, occupy disproportionately large cortical territory.
questions.keyConcept: S1 lies in the postcentral gyrus with an inverted contralateral sensory homunculus.
questions.modelAnswer: Site: the postcentral gyrus and the posterior part of the paracentral lobule. Body representation: an inverted sensory homunculus - the lower limb is represented medially (in the paracentral lobule), the trunk and upper limb in the middle, and the face laterally.

questions.text: Describe the functions and the effect of a lesion of Somatosensory Area 2 (S2). (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: The secondary somatosensory area (S2) lies in the parietal operculum and receives bilateral sensory input, unlike the strictly contralateral S1. It contributes to crude touch, pain and temperature perception and to integrative functions like recognising objects by touch. Because its representation is bilateral, lesions cause difficulty recognising or localising stimuli on both sides of the body.
questions.keyConcept: S2 processes bilateral pain, temperature and crude touch with higher-order tactile recognition.
questions.modelAnswer: Functions: S2 is involved in the perception of pain, temperature and crude touch, and contributes to higher-order sensory processing such as tactile recognition and sensory memory. Lesion effect: impairment in recognising or localising stimuli, affecting both sides of the body (bilateral effects).

questions.text: In infants, the spinal cord typically ends at which level?
questions.explanation: In newborns the spinal cord extends down to the L3 vertebral level because the vertebral column elongates faster than the cord during growth. By adulthood the conus medullaris ascends to the L1–L2 level.
questions.keyConcept: In infants the spinal cord ends at the L3 vertebral level.

questions.text: The subarachnoid space of the spinal cord ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The dural sac and the spinal subarachnoid space extend down to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). This lies well below the conus medullaris, so a lumbar puncture below L2 safely enters CSF around the cauda equina.
questions.keyConcept: The spinal subarachnoid space terminates at the S2 vertebral level.

questions.text: Which spinal level gives rise to the sympathetic white rami communicantes?
questions.explanation: White rami communicantes carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers and exist only at the thoracolumbar levels T1–L2. Of the options listed, only T5 falls within this sympathetic outflow.
questions.keyConcept: White rami communicantes occur only at thoracolumbar levels T1–L2.

questions.text: S2 spinal segment lies opposite to level of …… vertebra
questions.explanation: Because the spinal cord is shorter than the vertebral column, the sacral cord segments lie opposite the first lumbar (L1) vertebra. This vertebra–segment mismatch increases progressively toward the conus.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral cord segments lie opposite the L1 vertebra.

questions.text: Both rami of …… spinal nerve are purely motor
questions.explanation: The first cervical (C1, suboccipital) nerve usually has no dorsal sensory root. Therefore both its anterior and posterior rami are purely motor.
questions.keyConcept: Both rami of the C1 spinal nerve are purely motor.

questions.text: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers lies at ……
questions.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons occupy the lateral horn of the cord from T1 to L2. L2 is the lowest level among the choices that still contains this outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons span the T1–L2 lateral horn.

questions.text: A patient sustains a fracture of the T4 vertebra. Which spinal cord segment is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: In the upper thoracic region the cord segment lies about two levels below the same-numbered vertebra. A fracture of the T4 vertebra therefore injures the T6 cord segment.
questions.keyConcept: Upper-thoracic vertebrae overlie cord segments roughly two levels lower.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs is matched correctly in the motor hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Parietal association areas 5 and 7 integrate somatosensory input to provide awareness of body position in space. The other pairings are wrong because area 4 governs voluntary movement, area 6 motor planning, and area 17 vision.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal areas 5 and 7 mediate awareness of body position in space.
options: Areas 5 and 7 –awareness of body position in space

questions.text: Damage to which brain area typically causes sensory aphasia
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area, in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, is responsible for comprehension of language. Damage to it produces receptive (sensory) aphasia with fluent but meaningless speech.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke's area damage causes receptive (sensory) aphasia.

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding the representation in the somatosensory area one S1?
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory cortex receives crossed input, so each S1 represents the opposite half of the face and body. This contralateral organization is the correct statement among the options.

Face sensation is represented anteriorly, and body sensation is represented posteriorly
Face and body sensation is represented contralaterally

questions.text: Which cortical area(s) is/are located in the postcentral gyrus?
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory cortex comprising Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2 occupies the postcentral gyrus. Areas 5/7 and 39/40 lie further back in the parietal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2 form the postcentral gyrus.
options: Supra marginal gyrus (area 40) and angular gyrus (Area 39)

questions.text: Primary sensory cortex is present in which of the following areas?
questions.explanation: The postcentral gyrus continues onto the medial surface as the posterior part of the paracentral lobule. This region represents primary sensation from the contralateral lower limb.

questions.text: Contralateral representation of face and body is founded in ……
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory area (S1) contains the sensory homunculus for the contralateral face and body. It is the cortical site of contralateral sensory representation.
questions.keyConcept: S1 holds the contralateral sensory homunculus of face and body.

questions.explanation: GABA opens chloride channels, increasing Cl- influx and hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic membrane. This produces inhibitory postsynaptic potentials.

questions.text: Postsynaptic inhibition in the central nervous system is primarily mediated by which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glycine is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter mediating postsynaptic inhibition in the spinal cord. It opens chloride channels to hyperpolarize the postsynaptic neuron.
questions.keyConcept: Glycine mediates postsynaptic inhibition in the central nervous system.

questions.text: Which response occurs in a stretch reflex?
questions.explanation: In the stretch reflex, stretching a muscle excites its spindle afferents and reflexively contracts the same (agonist) muscle. Reciprocal inhibition simultaneously relaxes the antagonist.
questions.keyConcept: The stretch reflex contracts the stretched agonist muscle.

questions.text: Which of the following statements best describes sensory adaptation?
questions.explanation: Sensory adaptation is the progressive decline in receptor response despite a maintained stimulus. It allows the nervous system to ignore constant, unchanging stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory adaptation is diminished response to a continuous stimulus.

questions.text: BIO: Histamine is formed from histidine by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Histamine is produced from histidine by the enzyme histidine decarboxylase, which removes the carboxyl group. This decarboxylation reaction requires pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine is formed from histidine by decarboxylation.

questions.text: BIO: Neurons uptake glucose from the circulation through which of the following?
questions.explanation: Neurons take up glucose mainly through the high-affinity transporter GLUT3, allowing efficient uptake even at low glucose levels. GLUT1 instead serves the blood-brain barrier and glia.
questions.keyConcept: Neurons take up glucose via GLUT3.

questions.text: BIO: What is the inborn error of branched chain amino acids metabolism?
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease results from a defect in branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, impairing catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine. Accumulated keto acids give the urine a characteristic sweet odor.
questions.keyConcept: Maple syrup urine disease is the inborn error of branched-chain amino acid metabolism.

questions.text: BIO: Which of the following is/are allosteric activator(s) of glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by ADP and GDP, signalling a low-energy state that favors amino acid oxidation. GTP and ATP act as inhibitors of the enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: ADP and GDP allosterically activate glutamate dehydrogenase.

questions.text: BIO: Which of the following releases free ammonia?
questions.explanation: Catabolism of amino acids releases free ammonia, largely through oxidative deamination of glutamate. The biosynthetic reactions listed instead consume amide or amino nitrogen rather than liberating free ammonia.
questions.keyConcept: Amino acid catabolism releases free ammonia.

questions.text: BIO: Which of the following results from decrease of Gamma Amino Butyric Acid (GABA) synthesis?
questions.explanation: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter, so reduced GABA synthesis lowers inhibition and produces convulsions. This is why vitamin B6 deficiency, which impairs GABA formation, can cause seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Decreased GABA synthesis causes convulsions.

questions.text: BIO: Which one of the following enzymes is stimulated by cortisol in epinephrine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex induces phenylethanolamine N-methyl transferase (PNMT), which converts norepinephrine to epinephrine. This links adrenal medullary and cortical function.
questions.keyConcept: Cortisol stimulates N-methyl transferase (PNMT) in epinephrine synthesis.

questions.text: BIO: Which one of the following LDH isoenzymes is expressed in neurons?
questions.explanation: Neurons express LDH1, the isoenzyme composed of four H subunits suited to aerobic tissues. It favors conversion of lactate back to pyruvate for oxidative metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Neurons express the LDH1 isoenzyme.

questions.text: BIO: Methyl THF is used in synthesis of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Methyl-tetrahydrofolate donates its methyl group, via vitamin B12, to convert homocysteine into methionine. This reaction also regenerates free tetrahydrofolate.
questions.keyConcept: Methyl-THF supplies the methyl group to form methionine from homocysteine.

questions.text: BIO: The active form of folate is the carrier of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Tetrahydrofolate, the active form of folate, carries and transfers one-carbon units at various oxidation levels. These units are used in nucleotide and amino acid synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Active folate carries one-carbon units.

questions.text: BIO: Which of the following is caused by niacin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency causes pellagra, classically presenting with dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia. Niacin is a precursor of the coenzymes NAD and NADP.
questions.keyConcept: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra.

questions.text: BIO: Which of the following is caused by thiamin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Thiamin (vitamin B1) deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Thiamin pyrophosphate is a coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamin deficiency causes beriberi.

questions.text: BIO: Which of the following is/are the end product(s) of urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The cleavage of arginine by arginase yields urea and ornithine, while the preceding cleavage of argininosuccinate releases fumarate. The recognized end products of the cycle are therefore urea and fumarate.
questions.keyConcept: The end products of the urea cycle are urea and fumarate.

questions.text: BIO: Which one of the following compounds is a link between citric acid cycle and urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Fumarate produced in the urea cycle can enter the citric acid cycle, linking the two pathways. There it is converted to malate and then oxaloacetate.
questions.keyConcept: Fumarate links the urea cycle to the citric acid cycle.

questions.text: BIO: Which one of the following enzymes catalyzes this reaction: CO2 + NH3 + 2ATP yields carbamoyl phosphate?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, a mitochondrial enzyme, combines ammonia, carbon dioxide and two ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate. This is the committed first step of the urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I forms carbamoyl phosphate in the urea cycle.

questions.text: BIO: Which one of the following is required for the conversion of phenylalanine into tyrosine?
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine using tetrahydrobiopterin as the essential cofactor. Deficiency of this system causes phenylketonuria.
questions.keyConcept: Tetrahydrobiopterin is required to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine.

questions.text: Ammonia produced during amino acid catabolism is eliminated through the urea cycle. (a) Name the enzyme catalyzing the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle. (b) Name the allosteric activator of this enzyme. (c) Enumerate the sources of the urea nitrogen atoms. (3 Marks)
questions.explanation: The urea cycle disposes of toxic ammonia by incorporating two nitrogen atoms into urea. CPS I catalyses the committed, rate-limiting first step in the mitochondria and is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate, whose level rises when amino acid catabolism increases. The two urea nitrogens are derived from free ammonia and from aspartate.
questions.keyConcept: The urea cycle removes ammonia using nitrogens from free ammonia and aspartate.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Rate-limiting enzyme: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I). (b) Allosteric activator: N-acetylglutamate. (c) Sources of urea nitrogen atoms: the first nitrogen comes from free ammonia (NH3), and the second nitrogen comes from the amino group of aspartate in the cytosol.

questions.text: Describe the regulation of the urea cycle. (3 Marks)
questions.explanation: Urea cycle activity is matched to the nitrogen load that must be excreted. In the short term, N-acetylglutamate (made from glutamate and acetyl-CoA) allosterically activates CPS I. Over days, a high dietary protein intake or prolonged fasting increases transcription of all the urea cycle enzymes, raising the cycle's overall capacity.
questions.keyConcept: The urea cycle is regulated short-term by N-acetylglutamate and long-term by dietary protein.
questions.modelAnswer: Short-term (allosteric) regulation: N-acetylglutamate is an allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, so its concentration controls flux through the cycle. Long-term (adaptive) regulation: the synthesis of the urea cycle enzymes is induced or repressed according to dietary protein intake.

questions.text: Describe the biochemical basis of the following: (a) Methotrexate. (b) L-dopa in Parkinsonism. (3 Marks)
questions.explanation: Both answers rest on enzyme and transport specificity. Methotrexate is a folate analogue that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate and starving rapidly dividing cells of nucleotides. L-dopa is used instead of dopamine because dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, whereas its precursor can and is then converted to dopamine centrally.
questions.keyConcept: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier to replace dopamine.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Methotrexate is an anticancer drug that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking regeneration of tetrahydrofolate and therefore halting the nucleotide (purine and thymidylate) synthesis needed for cell division. (b) L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier (unlike dopamine), where it is decarboxylated to dopamine, restoring the dopamine/acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia that is lost in Parkinsonism.

questions.text: What is the importance of the astrocyte-neuron (lactate) shuttle? (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: The astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle couples neuronal activity to energy supply. Astrocytes, which contact the capillaries, perform glycolysis and export lactate that neurons take up and oxidise for ATP. This provides neurons with a rapid fuel during intense synaptic activity.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes supply neurons with lactate as a rapid energy source during activity.
questions.modelAnswer: Astrocytes take up glucose from the blood and convert it to lactate. This lactate is then shuttled to neurons, where it is used as a primary energy source, particularly during periods of high neuronal activity.

questions.text: Why does Vitamin B6 deficiency cause convulsions? (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the CNS and is made from glutamate by the B6-dependent enzyme glutamate decarboxylase. When pyridoxal phosphate is deficient, GABA levels drop while excitatory activity is unopposed. The resulting imbalance toward excitation lowers the seizure threshold and produces convulsions.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B6 deficiency lowers GABA synthesis, causing neuronal over-excitation and convulsions.
questions.modelAnswer: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) is a required cofactor for the synthesis of GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter. In its deficiency, GABA synthesis falls, removing inhibitory tone and leading to neuronal over-excitation and hyperactivity that manifests as convulsions.

questions.text: A 53-year-old man presented with uncontrolled hypertension, severe headache, and palpitations. His urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) was 630 mg/day (normal 5 mg/day). (a) What is the most probable diagnosis? (b) What is the biochemical basis of the drug chosen for treatment (alpha-methyl tyrosine)? (c) What are the neurotransmitters synthesized from tyrosine? (3 Marks)
questions.explanation: The markedly elevated VMA (a catecholamine metabolite) together with hypertension, headache and palpitations is the classic picture of a pheochromocytoma. Alpha-methyl tyrosine works by blocking tyrosine hydroxylase, the committed rate-limiting step that converts tyrosine to L-DOPA, so the whole catecholamine pathway is reduced. That pathway sequentially produces dopamine, then norepinephrine, then epinephrine.
questions.keyConcept: Pheochromocytoma overproduces catecholamines; alpha-methyl tyrosine blocks the rate-limiting tyrosine hydroxylase.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Most probable diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma (a catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla). (b) Alpha-methyl tyrosine inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis, thereby reducing catecholamine production. (c) Neurotransmitters synthesised from tyrosine: dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and epinephrine (adrenaline).

questions.text: Enumerate the "brain fuels". (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: The brain has a high, continuous energy demand but very limited fuel storage. Under normal fed conditions it relies almost exclusively on glucose delivered by the blood. During prolonged fasting or starvation, ketone bodies produced by the liver become a major alternative fuel and spare glucose.
questions.keyConcept: The brain uses glucose normally and ketone bodies during prolonged fasting.
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose: the primary fuel of the brain under normal conditions. Ketone bodies (e.g., beta-hydroxybutyrate): used during prolonged fasting or starvation when glucose availability is limited.

questions.text: Mention the importance of Vitamin B3 (Niacin). (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: Vitamin B3 is incorporated into the nicotinamide nucleotides NAD+ and NADP+, the major electron carriers of catabolic and anabolic redox reactions. Adequate niacin is therefore essential for ATP generation in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Its deficiency produces pellagra, remembered as the three Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.
questions.keyConcept: Niacin forms the NAD/NADP coenzymes; its deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia).
questions.modelAnswer: Function: niacin is a precursor of NAD and NADP, which are essential coenzymes for redox reactions in energy metabolism (e.g., glycolysis and the Krebs cycle). Deficiency: leads to Pellagra, characterised by the 3 Ds - Dermatitis, Diarrhoea, and Dementia.

questions.text: Ammonia produced during amino acid catabolism is eliminated through the urea cycle. (1) Name the enzyme catalyzing the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle. (2) Name the allosteric activator of this enzyme. (3) Enumerate the sources of the urea nitrogen atoms.
questions.explanation: CPS I catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle and is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate. The two nitrogen atoms of urea are derived from free ammonia and from the amino group of aspartate.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I is the rate-limiting urea-cycle enzyme activated by N-acetylglutamate.
questions.modelAnswer: (1) Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I). (2) N-acetylglutamate. (3) The first nitrogen comes free as NH3, while the second nitrogen comes from aspartic acid in the cytosol.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymatic changes explains the slow rate of glycolysis in neurons?
questions.explanation: Neurons have reduced activity of 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase, lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, the main activator of phosphofructokinase-1. This slows the rate of glycolysis in neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Low fructose-2,6-bisphosphate slows neuronal glycolysis.
options: High activity of 6 phosphofructo 2 kinase which inhibit the formation of fructose 2,6 bisphosphate
Reduced activity of 6 phosphofructo 2 kinase with decreased fructose 2,6 bisphosphate
Reduced activity of hexokinase with decreased intracellular glucose
High activity of 6 phosphofructo 2 kinase which stimulate the formation of fructose 2,6 bisphosphate

questions.text: During excessive exercise, which substance serves as an energy source for neurons?
questions.explanation: During heavy exercise, lactate produced by muscle and astrocytes is taken up and oxidized by neurons for energy. This astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle supplements glucose use.
questions.keyConcept: Lactate serves as a neuronal energy source during heavy exercise.

questions.text: Which statement about ketone bodies is correct?
questions.explanation: Ketone bodies are not a major energy source in the well-fed state, when glucose predominates. They become important for the brain only during prolonged fasting.
questions.keyConcept: Ketone bodies are not a major fuel in the well-fed state.
options: Main energy source for the brain
Main energy source for the liver during starvation
Not a major source of energy in well-fed state

questions.text: During starvation, which of the following occurs?
questions.explanation: During starvation the brain adapts to utilize ketone bodies for energy. The liver produces ketone bodies but cannot use them because it lacks thiophorase.
questions.keyConcept: During starvation the brain utilizes ketone bodies.
options: Ketone bodies are utilized in liver
Ketone bodies are utilized in brain
Fatty acid are utilized in brain
Amino acid are utilized in brain

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is absent in neurons?
questions.explanation: Neurons lack 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (PFK2/FBPase2). Its absence keeps fructose-2,6-bisphosphate low and glycolysis slow.
questions.keyConcept: Neurons lack the PFK2/FBPase2 enzyme.

questions.text: Which of the following laboratory findings is used as a marker for carcinoid tumor?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumors secrete excess serotonin, which is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). Elevated urinary 5-HIAA is the diagnostic marker.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary 5-HIAA is the marker of carcinoid tumor.

questions.text: Which of the following neurotransmitters is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system. GABA and glycine are the main inhibitory transmitters.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate is the main excitatory CNS neurotransmitter.

questions.text: Which substance acts as an antioxidant in astrocytes by forming reduced glutathione?
questions.explanation: NADPH provides reducing power to regenerate reduced glutathione in astrocytes. This protects against oxidative damage as an antioxidant defense.
questions.keyConcept: NADPH regenerates reduced glutathione for antioxidant defense.

questions.text: In pheochromocytoma, which metabolite is typically increased in urine?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma overproduces catecholamines that are metabolized to vanillylmandelic acid. Elevated urinary VMA is characteristic.
questions.keyConcept: Pheochromocytoma raises urinary vanillylmandelic acid.

questions.text: Which of the following amino acids is the precursor of serotonin?
questions.explanation: Tryptophan is the amino acid precursor of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine). It is hydroxylated and decarboxylated to form serotonin.
questions.keyConcept: Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin.

questions.text: Which of the following drugs prevents the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine?
questions.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, preventing conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the brain. This increases central levodopa availability and reduces side effects.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine.

questions.text: Which of the following glucose transporters is present on astrocytes?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes express the GLUT1 glucose transporter. Neurons rely mainly on GLUT3.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes express the GLUT1 glucose transporter.

questions.text: Which of the following is the rate limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis. It converts tyrosine to DOPA.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting catecholamine enzyme.

questions.text: Which of the following effects is produced by carbidopa when given with L-DOPA?
questions.explanation: By inhibiting peripheral decarboxylation of L-DOPA, carbidopa increases the amount reaching the brain. This enhances the therapeutic action of L-DOPA.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa increases L-DOPA action centrally.
options: Increase dopamine breakdown in the brain

questions.text: GABA in postsynaptic nerve which increases the permeability of?
questions.explanation: GABA binding to postsynaptic GABA-A receptors increases chloride permeability. The resulting chloride influx hyperpolarizes the neuron and inhibits it.
questions.keyConcept: GABA increases postsynaptic chloride permeability.

questions.text: Deficiency or dysregulation of which of the following neurotransmitters is most closely associated with mood disorders?
questions.explanation: Deficiency or dysregulation of serotonin is most closely linked to mood disorders such as depression. This underlies the use of serotonergic antidepressants.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin dysregulation is closely associated with mood disorders.

questions.text: Which enzyme is classified as a transaminase?
questions.explanation: Alanine aminotransferase is a transaminase that transfers an amino group between alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate. Transaminases interconvert amino acids and keto acids.
questions.keyConcept: Alanine aminotransferase is a transaminase.

questions.text: Which of the following cofactors is required for transamination reactions?
questions.explanation: Transamination reactions require pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6, as a coenzyme. It carries the amino group during the reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Pyridoxal phosphate is the coenzyme for transamination.

questions.text: Which enzyme catalyzes transamination reactions in amino acid metabolism?
questions.explanation: Aspartate aminotransferase catalyzes transamination between aspartate and alpha-ketoglutarate. Like other transaminases it requires pyridoxal phosphate.
questions.keyConcept: Aspartate aminotransferase catalyzes a transamination reaction.

questions.text: Which of the following is the common amino acid acceptor in all transamination reactions?
questions.explanation: Alpha-ketoglutarate is the common amino-group acceptor in transamination reactions, becoming glutamate. This channels amino groups toward disposal.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-ketoglutarate is the universal transamination amino acceptor.

questions.text: Which enzyme is involved in transdeaminase?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase performs the oxidative deamination step of transdeamination, releasing free ammonia. It works after transaminases funnel amino groups into glutamate.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate dehydrogenase carries out oxidative deamination in transdeamination.

questions.text: Hyperammonemia is associated with …… in the brain
questions.explanation: Hyperammonemia raises brain tryptophan uptake and thereby increases serotonin synthesis. It also depletes alpha-ketoglutarate through glutamine formation, contributing to encephalopathy.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperammonemia is associated with increased brain serotonin.

questions.text: Which compound in the urea cycle requires ATP for its synthesis?
questions.explanation: Argininosuccinate synthesis from citrulline and aspartate consumes ATP in the urea cycle. This is one of the cycle's energy-requiring steps.
questions.keyConcept: Argininosuccinate synthesis in the urea cycle requires ATP.

questions.text: In a patient with a urea cycle disorder, which metabolite typically accumulates?
questions.explanation: In urea cycle disorders, ammonia is diverted into glutamine, which accumulates. Elevated glutamine reflects impaired ammonia disposal.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine accumulates in urea cycle disorders.

questions.text: Which of the following changes occurs in the brain as a result of hyperammonemia?
questions.explanation: In hyperammonemia ammonia is detoxified by combining with glutamate to form glutamine, depleting glutamate. Because GABA is synthesized from glutamate, both glutamate and GABA fall in the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperammonemia decreases brain glutamate and GABA.

questions.text: human body?
questions.explanation: Urea is the main nitrogen-containing excretory product of protein metabolism in humans. It is synthesized in the liver and excreted by the kidneys.
questions.keyConcept: Urea is the principal nitrogen excretory product in humans.

questions.text: In ornithine transcarbamylasedeficiency, which of the following amino acids becomes essential?
questions.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency blocks the urea cycle, so arginine can no longer be synthesized adequately and becomes essential. Supplementation helps maintain the cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine becomes essential in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

questions.text: The nitrogen atoms of urea are derived from which of the following sources?
questions.explanation: The two nitrogen atoms of urea come from free ammonia (via carbamoyl phosphate) and from aspartate. These enter the urea cycle at different steps.
questions.keyConcept: Urea nitrogen derives from ammonia and aspartate.

questions.text: Which of the following amino acids are responsible for the characteristic burned sugar odor of urine?
questions.explanation: The branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine accumulate in maple syrup urine disease. Their keto acids give urine the characteristic burnt-sugar (maple syrup) odor.
questions.keyConcept: Branched-chain amino acids cause the maple-syrup urine odor.

questions.text: A mother notices that her month-old baby’s urine has a sweet, burnt sugar smell while changing the diaper. Laboratory tests reveal elevated levels of leucine, isoleucine, and valine in the blood. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease is caused by deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This blocks degradation of leucine, isoleucine and valine.
questions.keyConcept: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease.

questions.text: Which of the following reactions is impaired in thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids such as pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate. Its deficiency impairs these dehydrogenase reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine deficiency impairs oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids.
options: Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha keto acids

questions.text: In phenylketonuria, …… in the brain.
questions.explanation: In phenylketonuria, excess phenylalanine inhibits tyrosine and dopamine synthesis, lowering brain dopamine. This contributes to the neurological impairment.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylketonuria decreases brain dopamine.

questions.text: In phenylketonuria, which substance accumulates in the blood?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine accumulates in the blood. The excess is toxic to the developing brain.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylalanine accumulates in the blood in phenylketonuria.

questions.text: Which of the following disease and metabolite pairs is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria is correctly matched with accumulation of phenylalanine. Maple syrup urine disease accumulates branched-chain amino acids, not the options listed.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylketonuria is characterized by accumulation of phenylalanine.
options: Maple syrup urine disease and isolysin
Maple syrup urine disease and lysin
Maple syrup urine disease and glycine

questions.text: In phenylketonuria, deficiency of which of the following substances occurs?
questions.explanation: Because phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine, synthesis of catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) is reduced. This catecholamine deficiency affects the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylketonuria causes catecholamine deficiency.

questions.text: A 55 year-old chronic alcoholic presents with confusion, ataxia, and memory impairment. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for his presentation?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcoholism with confusion, ataxia and memory loss indicates Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency. It is a classic clinical triad.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.text: A 55 year-old chronic alcoholic presents with confusion, ataxia, and memory impairment. Which of the following enzymes if affected?
questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency impairs the thiamine-dependent alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase of the citric acid cycle. Reduced activity limits brain energy production.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine deficiency impairs alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is required for one carbon transfer reactions involved in nucleotide synthesis?
questions.explanation: Folic acid carries one-carbon units required for purine and thymidylate (nucleotide) synthesis. Its deficiency impairs DNA synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Folic acid supplies one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis.

questions.text: Impairment of oxidative decarboxylation leads to inability to utilize glucose due to deficiency of which pf the following?
questions.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, which decarboxylates pyruvate for glucose oxidation. Its deficiency blocks glucose utilization.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine deficiency impairs oxidative decarboxylation needed for glucose use.

questions.text: A patient presents with chronic diarrhea, cognitive decline, and photosensitive skin rash. Which supplement should you indicate to this patient?
questions.explanation: Diarrhea, dementia and a photosensitive dermatitis are the classic triad of pellagra from niacin deficiency. Niacin supplementation is the treatment.
questions.keyConcept: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra (diarrhea, dementia, dermatitis).

questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency is neurologically affected by folic acid status, as folic acid supplementation can mask its hematological signs but not prevent neurological damage?
questions.explanation: Folate supplementation can correct the megaloblastic anemia of vitamin B12 deficiency while the neurological damage progresses. B12 deficiency therefore has masked hematologic but unprevented neurologic effects.
questions.keyConcept: Folate masks the anemia but not neuropathy of B12 deficiency.

questions.text: Which biochemical process is inhibited by sulfonamides?
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides inhibit bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folic acid synthesis. Humans obtain folate from the diet, giving selective toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Sulfonamides inhibit bacterial folic acid synthesis.

questions.text: Which vitamins are directly required for the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine?
questions.explanation: Remethylation of homocysteine to methionine requires methyl-tetrahydrofolate and vitamin B12 (methylcobalamin). Both vitamins are needed for the methionine synthase reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Folate and vitamin B12 remethylate homocysteine to methionine.

questions.text: Which reaction uses methyl tetrahydrofolate as a cofactor?
questions.explanation: Methyl-tetrahydrofolate donates its methyl group during conversion of homocysteine to methionine. Vitamin B12 transfers this methyl group.
questions.keyConcept: Methyl-tetrahydrofolate is used in homocysteine remethylation to methionine.

questions.text: Which of the following acts as a coenzyme for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases?
questions.explanation: Tetrahydrobiopterin is the coenzyme for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases such as phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylase. It supplies reducing equivalents for hydroxylation.
questions.keyConcept: Tetrahydrobiopterin is the coenzyme for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases.

questions.text: The conversion of which of the following requires vitamin B12 and folic acid?
questions.explanation: Conversion of homocysteine to methionine requires both folic acid (as methyl-tetrahydrofolate) and vitamin B12. Deficiency of either raises homocysteine.
questions.keyConcept: Homocysteine-to-methionine conversion needs folate and vitamin B12.

questions.text: A demyelinating lesion is observed in a patient with Multiple Sclerosis. Which adult cell population is most likely to remyelinate the axons?
questions.explanation: Within the CNS, adult oligodendrocyte progenitor cells can differentiate into oligodendrocytes and remyelinate denuded axons. Schwann cells myelinate the peripheral, not central, nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Adult oligodendrocyte progenitors remyelinate CNS axons.

questions.text: A pathologist stains brain tissue using GFAP. Which glial cell is being evaluated?
questions.explanation: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is the intermediate filament marker of astrocytes. It is widely used to identify astrocytes and astrocytic tumors.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP is the histological marker of astrocytes.

questions.text: In a patient with CNS inflammation, microglial cells are observed in an activated state. Which function do these cells primarily perform?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the CNS and, when activated, act as phagocytes that engulf debris and pathogens. They do not form myelin or release neurotransmitters.
questions.keyConcept: Activated microglia perform phagocytosis in the CNS.

questions.text: The blood-brain barrier lacks protection in all of the following regions except:
questions.explanation: Circumventricular organs such as the pineal body, posterior pituitary, choroid plexus and parts of the hypothalamus lack a complete blood-brain barrier. The cerebral cortex retains an intact barrier.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebral cortex has an intact blood-brain barrier.

questions.text: The horizontal cells of Cajal are located in which layer of the cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: Horizontal cells of Cajal are found in the most superficial molecular (plexiform) layer of the cortex. Their axons run horizontally within this layer.
questions.keyConcept: Horizontal cells of Cajal lie in the molecular layer.

questions.text: Which cell type lines the ventricles of the brain and contributes to CSF circulation?
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells form the ciliated epithelium lining the ventricles and central canal. Their cilia help circulate cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and move CSF.

questions.text: Which cerebral cortex cell type is found in all layers and has ascending axons?
questions.explanation: Cells of Martinotti occur in all cortical layers and send their axons upward toward the molecular layer. This ascending axon is their distinguishing feature.
questions.keyConcept: Cells of Martinotti occur in all layers with ascending axons.

questions.text: Which CNS region contains protoplasmic astrocytes as the predominant glial type?
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes predominate in the gray matter, whereas fibrous astrocytes are characteristic of white matter. Their many short branching processes contact neurons and capillaries.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes predominate in gray matter.

questions.text: Which glial cell type in the CNS is primarily responsible for forming the myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons within the CNS, each ensheathing several axons. Schwann cells perform the equivalent role only in the peripheral nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin.

questions.text: Which layer contains the giant pyramidal (Betz) cells?
questions.explanation: The giant pyramidal cells of Betz are located in the internal pyramidal layer (layer V) of the motor cortex. Their axons contribute to the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Betz cells lie in the internal pyramidal layer.

questions.text: Which of the following characteristics best distinguishes oligodendrocytes from Schwann cells?
questions.explanation: A single oligodendrocyte can myelinate several axons, whereas one Schwann cell myelinates only a single internode of one axon. Schwann cells, not oligodendrocytes, are derived from neural crest.
questions.keyConcept: One oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple axons.

questions.text: Which structure is formed by astrocyte foot processes and contributes to selective permeability in CNS capillaries?
questions.explanation: Perivascular astrocyte foot processes ensheath CNS capillaries and help induce and maintain the blood-brain barrier. They contribute to its selective permeability.
questions.keyConcept: Perivascular astrocyte feet support the blood-brain barrier.

questions.text: Describe the structure, type, functions, and clinical relevance of astrocytes in the CNS.
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cells and provide structural and metabolic support to neurons. Their foot processes contact capillaries to help form and maintain the blood-brain barrier, while GFAP gives them their characteristic cytoskeleton and serves as a diagnostic marker. Following injury they proliferate to form a glial scar.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes are GFAP-positive glia that support neurons and maintain the blood-brain barrier.
questions.modelAnswer: Structure: star-shaped cells with foot processes, GFAP-positive intermediate filaments, and glycogen storage. Types: fibrous astrocytes (mainly white matter) and protoplasmic astrocytes (mainly gray matter). Functions: maintenance of the blood-brain barrier, ionic balance, metabolic support, repair by glial scar formation, and neurotransmitter regulation. Clinical relevance: GFAP is a diagnostic marker in astrocytoma.

questions.text: Describe the six layers of the cerebral cortex with their components.
questions.explanation: The neocortex is organised into six horizontal layers distinguished by their predominant cell types and fibre bands. Granular layers (2 and 4) are rich in small stellate or granule cells that receive input, while pyramidal layers (3 and 5) contain output neurons, including the giant pyramidal (Betz) cells of the motor cortex. The bands of Baillarger are horizontal myelinated fibre plexuses within the granular and pyramidal layers.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebral cortex has six layers alternating granular and pyramidal cell populations.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Molecular layer: horizontal cells of Cajal and tangential fibres. 2) External granular layer: small granule cells. 3) External pyramidal layer: small and medium pyramidal cells. 4) Internal granular layer: granule cells and the outer band of Baillarger. 5) Internal pyramidal layer: giant pyramidal cells and the inner band of Baillarger. 6) Multiform (pleomorphic) layer: fusiform and granule cells.

questions.text: Discuss the types, structure and functions of astrocytes.
questions.explanation: Astrocytes exist as fibrous and protoplasmic types adapted to white and gray matter respectively. Their perivascular foot processes and GFAP-rich cytoplasm allow them to support the blood-brain barrier and buffer the neuronal microenvironment. They also store glycogen and respond to injury by forming a glial scar.
questions.keyConcept: Fibrous and protoplasmic astrocytes support neurons, the blood-brain barrier, and ionic balance.
questions.modelAnswer: Types: fibrous astrocytes (mainly white matter) and protoplasmic astrocytes (mainly gray matter). Structure: star-shaped cells with a large nucleus and cytoplasm containing GFAP, microtubules and glycogen; processes end as astrocytic feet contacting blood vessels. Functions: regulate metabolic exchange, maintain extracellular ionic balance, form part of the blood-brain barrier, repair by glial scar formation, and store glycogen.

questions.text: Explain the components and significance of the blood-brain barrier.
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier is formed mainly by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells, reinforced by a basement membrane, pericytes and astrocytic foot processes. This structural arrangement makes the barrier highly selective, blocking most large or charged molecules and pathogens. It thereby protects the CNS and keeps the extracellular environment tightly regulated for neuronal function.
questions.keyConcept: The blood-brain barrier uses tight-junctioned endothelium, basement membrane, pericytes, and astrocytic feet to protect the brain.
questions.modelAnswer: Components: 1) continuous endothelial cells joined by tight junctions; 2) a continuous basement membrane; 3) pericytes; 4) astrocytic end-feet. Significance: it selectively restricts the passage of substances from blood to brain, protecting neural tissue from toxins and pathogens while allowing essential nutrients such as glucose and oxygen to cross, thereby maintaining a stable neuronal environment.

questions.text: Differentiate between motor and sensory cortex based on cellular composition.
questions.explanation: Cortical regions are described as agranular or granular depending on the balance of pyramidal output cells and granule input cells. The motor cortex is agranular and thick, dominated by large pyramidal cells that give rise to descending motor fibres. The sensory cortex is granular and thinner, rich in granule cells suited to receiving and processing afferent input.
questions.keyConcept: Motor cortex is pyramidal-rich and agranular; sensory cortex is granule-rich and granular.
questions.modelAnswer: Motor cortex (agranular): thicker, with prominent pyramidal cells (including giant Betz cells) and few granule cells. Sensory cortex (granular): thinner, with prominent granule (granular) cells and very few pyramidal cells.

questions.text: Enumerate the six histological layers of the cerebral cortex.
questions.explanation: From the surface inward, the neocortex consists of six named layers. These alternate between granular layers (external and internal granular) and pyramidal layers (external and internal pyramidal), bounded superficially by the molecular layer and deeply by the multiform layer. This six-layered pattern (isocortex) is characteristic of most of the cerebral cortex.
questions.keyConcept: The six cortical layers: molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal, multiform.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Molecular layer. 2) External granular layer. 3) External pyramidal layer. 4) Internal granular layer. 5) Internal pyramidal layer. 6) Multiform (pleomorphic) layer.

questions.text: Which cell is involved in the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB), and what is its intermediate filament? (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells, supported by the foot processes of astrocytes that induce and maintain the barrier. Astrocytes are identified histologically by their characteristic intermediate filament, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). GFAP staining is widely used to demonstrate astrocytes and reactive gliosis.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes support the blood-brain barrier and contain the intermediate filament GFAP.
questions.modelAnswer: Cell: the astrocyte (its perivascular foot processes). Intermediate filament: Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP).

questions.text: Enumerate the central glia (neuroglia). (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: The central neuroglia are the supporting cells of the CNS, each with a distinct role. Astrocytes provide metabolic and structural support and contribute to the blood-brain barrier, while oligodendrocytes produce the myelin sheaths of central axons. Microglia act as the resident phagocytes and immune cells, and ependymal cells line the ventricular system and help circulate cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Central glia are astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and ependymal cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Astrocytes (support and form the blood-brain barrier). Oligodendrocytes (myelinate CNS axons). Microglia (phagocytic immune cells). Ependymal cells (line the ventricles).

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding neuroglia?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes proliferate to form glial scar tissue (gliosis) after central nervous system injury. Oligodendrocytes, not astrocytes or microglia, produce central myelin.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes perform gliosis after CNS injury.
options: Oligodendrocytes form the blood brain barrier
Schwann cells are found in the central nervous system
Ependymal cells form nodes of Ranvier

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the layers of the cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger lies within the inner granular (fourth) layer of the cerebral cortex. These bands are horizontal myelinated fiber plexuses.
questions.keyConcept: The outer band of Baillarger lies in the inner granular layer.
options: The outer band of Baillargeris present in the inner granular layer
The inner band of Baillargeris present in the molecular layer
The molecular layer contains large pyramidal cells
The inner granular layer lacks stellate cells
The multiform layer is the most superficial layer

questions.text: Define neuroglia.
questions.modelAnswer: Neuroglia are the interstitial supporting cells of the nervous tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroglia are the interstitial supporting cells of the nervous tissue.
questions.explanation: Neuroglia, also known as glial cells, play a crucial role in supporting and maintaining the structure and function of the nervous system. They provide nutrients, remove waste products, and offer physical support to neurons, allowing them to function optimally. In the context of histology, neuroglia are an essential component of the nervous tissue, and their proper identification and understanding are vital for medical students to comprehend the complex relationships between neurons and their supporting cells.

questions.text: Mention the histological components of the CNS.
questions.modelAnswer: Histologically, CNS is formed of nerve cells (neurons), supporting cells (neuroglia), and blood capillaries.
questions.keyConcept: The central nervous system (CNS) is composed of three primary histological components.
questions.explanation: The CNS is formed of nerve cells (neurons), which are responsible for transmitting and processing information, while supporting cells (neuroglia) provide structural and functional support to neurons. Blood capillaries are also present, supplying the CNS with oxygen and nutrients. These components work together to enable the complex functions of the CNS, including control of the body's functions and maintenance of homeostasis.

questions.text: How can neuroglia be seen in ordinary and special stains?
questions.modelAnswer:
In H&E-stained sections, only the nuclei of neuroglia can be seen.
Neuroglia can be detected by silver or gold impregnation methods.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroglia can be visualized in histological sections using specific staining techniques.
questions.explanation: In routine H&E-stained sections, only the nuclei of neuroglia are visible due to the limited staining capabilities of this method. However, specialized staining techniques such as silver or gold impregnation can highlight the entire cell, including the cytoplasm and processes of neuroglia, allowing for their detection and identification. This is particularly useful in diagnosing conditions affecting the central nervous system, where neuroglia play a crucial role in maintaining tissue integrity and function.

questions.text: Classify neuroglia according to site.
questions.modelAnswer:
In the CNS, neuroglia include oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells.
In the PNS, they include Schwann cells and satellite cells.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroglia can be classified into two main categories based on their location: central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS).
questions.explanation: This classification is essential in understanding the distinct roles and functions of different types of neuroglia in the CNS and PNS. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells play crucial roles in myelination, support, immune response, and cerebrospinal fluid production, respectively. In contrast, the PNS contains Schwann cells and satellite cells, which are responsible for myelination and supporting neurons, respectively.

questions.text: Describe the origin and site of oligodendrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer: Oligodendrocytes are ectodermal in origin and are found in the white matter of the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes are ectodermal in origin and are found in the white matter of the CNS.
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are a type of glial cell in the central nervous system (CNS) that are responsible for myelinating neurons. They originate from the ectoderm, one of the three primary germ layers that form during embryonic development. Specifically, oligodendrocytes are found in the white matter of the CNS, which is composed of myelinated nerve fibers that facilitate rapid transmission of electrical signals.

questions.text: Describe the shape of oligodendrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer:
They are small cells with rounded dark nuclei.
Their thin cytoplasmic processes are filled with microtubules but lack intermediate filaments and glycogen.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes have a distinctive shape characterized by thin cytoplasmic processes.
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are a type of glial cell in the central nervous system that are responsible for myelinating neurons. Their unique shape, with thin cytoplasmic processes filled with microtubules, allows them to efficiently wrap around axons to form the myelin sheath, facilitating the transmission of electrical signals. This distinct morphology is a key feature that distinguishes oligodendrocytes from other types of glial cells.

questions.text: Explain how oligodendrocytes form myelin in the CNS.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each process becomes sheet-like and wraps repeatedly around a portion of a nearby axon, forming the
myelin sheath in the CNS. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate up to 60 axons.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS by wrapping their processes around axons.
questions.explanation: In the central nervous system (CNS), oligodendrocytes play a crucial role in myelination by extending their processes to wrap around axons, forming a compact, insulating sheath known as the myelin sheath. This process allows for the rapid transmission of electrical signals along the axon, facilitating communication between neurons. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate up to 60 axons, making them highly efficient in their role.

questions.text: Mention the functions of oligodendrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer:
They myelinate nerve fibers in the CNS, form myelin sheaths of several internodal segments on the same or
different axons, support neurons, and insulate nerve impulses.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes play a crucial role in the central nervous system (CNS) by myelinating nerve fibers.
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are a type of glial cell in the CNS that are responsible for myelinating nerve fibers, which is essential for the rapid transmission of nerve impulses. By forming myelin sheaths, oligodendrocytes increase the speed of nerve conduction and facilitate the insulation of nerve impulses, allowing for efficient communication between neurons. This process is vital for maintaining proper neural function and is a key feature of oligodendrocyte biology.

questions.text: Which cells are affected in multiple sclerosis?
questions.modelAnswer:
Multiple sclerosis is chronic inflammation of the CNS characterized by loss of myelin due to destruction of
Oligodendrocytes.
During active disease, T lymphocytes initiate inflammation with loss of oligodendrocytes and axon
demyelination in white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by the destruction of oligodendrocytes, leading to demyelination in the CNS.
questions.explanation: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system mistakenly attacks the protective myelin sheath surrounding nerve fibers in the central nervous system (CNS), leading to the destruction of oligodendrocytes, the cells responsible for myelin production. This destruction results in demyelination, where the myelin sheath is lost, disrupting nerve signal transmission. The loss of oligodendrocytes is a critical aspect of the disease pathology, as it leads to the characteristic symptoms of multiple sclerosis, including vision loss, muscle weakness, and cognitive impairment.

questions.text: Describe the origin and site of astrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Astrocytes are ectodermal in origin. They are present in white and gray matter and are the most numerous
glial cells in gray matter.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes originate from the ectodermal layer of the neural tube.
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are a type of glial cell that arises from the ectodermal layer of the neural tube during embryonic development. This ectodermal origin is distinct from other glial cells, such as oligodendrocytes, which have a different developmental lineage. As a result, astrocytes are found in both white and gray matter, with the highest concentration in gray matter, where they play a crucial role in maintaining the extracellular environment and supporting neuronal function.

questions.text: Describe the general shape of astrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Astrocytes are star-like cells. Their processes end by expanded parts called astrocyte feet, which contact
blood capillaries, neurons, or nerve fibers. Astrocytes are connected by gap junctions and have large ovoid
or rounded nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes have a star-like shape with expanded processes called astrocyte feet that contact surrounding cells and blood vessels.
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are a type of glial cell in the central nervous system that play a crucial role in maintaining the environment surrounding neurons. Their star-like shape allows them to extend their processes to contact blood capillaries, neurons, and nerve fibers, facilitating the exchange of nutrients and waste products. The expanded parts of their processes, known as astrocyte feet, are particularly important for this function, enabling astrocytes to regulate the local environment and support neuronal health.

questions.text: List the cytoplasmic contents of astrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Their cytoplasm contains microtubules, intermediate glial filaments formed of GFAP, thread-like
mitochondria, and glycogen.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes contain a unique set of cytoplasmic components that support their role in the central nervous system.
questions.explanation: Astrocytes, a type of glial cell in the brain and spinal cord, are characterized by their distinctive cytoplasmic contents. These include microtubules, which provide structural support, intermediate filaments formed of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), which gives the cell its characteristic appearance, and thread-like mitochondria, which generate energy for the cell. Additionally, astrocytes contain glycogen, a complex carbohydrate that serves as a readily available energy source, highlighting their role in supporting the metabolic needs of neurons.

questions.text: Classify astrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fibrous astrocytes are found in white matter and have long thin processes.
Protoplasmic astrocytes are found in gray matter and have short extensive processes.
Specialized astrocytes include Muller cells in the retina and pituicytes of the posterior pituitary.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes are a type of glial cell in the central nervous system that can be classified into different subtypes based on their morphology and location.
questions.explanation: Astrocytes play a crucial role in maintaining the health and function of neurons in the central nervous system. Fibrous astrocytes, found in white matter, have long thin processes that facilitate the transmission of signals, whereas protoplasmic astrocytes, found in gray matter, have short extensive processes that allow for nutrient and waste exchange. Specialized astrocytes, such as Muller cells in the retina and pituicytes in the posterior pituitary, have unique functions and morphologies that adapt to their specific locations within the nervous system.

questions.text: Mention 5 functions of astrocytes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Astrocytes secrete factors regulating neural functions, support neurons, store glycogen that can be broken
down to glucose and lactate for neurons, repair by proliferation and glial scar formation, and form part of
the blood-brain barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes play a multifaceted role in the central nervous system, encompassing various functions beyond mere support.
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are a type of glial cell that perform a range of critical functions, including the secretion of factors that regulate neural functions, support of neurons through the provision of nutrients and oxygen, and the storage of glycogen that can be broken down to glucose and lactate for the energy needs of neurons. Additionally, astrocytes are involved in the repair of damaged neural tissue through proliferation and the formation of glial scars, and they contribute to the integrity of the blood-brain barrier, which is essential for maintaining the unique environment of the central nervous system.

questions.text: Describe the origin, site, and shape of microglia.
questions.modelAnswer:
Microglia originate from blood monocytes. They are found in gray and white matter of the brain and spinal
cord, retina, and optic nerve. They are small spindle-shaped cells with branching poles, minute surface
spines, dense elongated nuclei, and scanty cytoplasm.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are small, spindle-shaped cells that originate from blood monocytes.
questions.explanation: Microglia are a type of glial cell that play a crucial role in the immune response within the central nervous system. They are derived from circulating blood monocytes that migrate into the brain and spinal cord, where they differentiate into microglia. This unique origin and function allow microglia to act as the first line of defense against pathogens and injury in the central nervous system.

questions.text: Mention the functions of microglia.
questions.modelAnswer:
Microglia are the phagocytes of the CNS.
They express receptors for neurotransmitters and may influence synaptic transmission.
During development, they remove apoptotic cells.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia serve as the primary phagocytic cells in the central nervous system (CNS).
questions.explanation: Microglia play a crucial role in maintaining the health of the CNS by acting as phagocytes, engulfing and removing dead cells, foreign substances, and other debris. This function is essential for preventing the accumulation of toxic waste and promoting a healthy environment for neuronal function. Additionally, microglia express receptors for neurotransmitters, which allows them to modulate synaptic transmission and influence the surrounding neural environment.

questions.text: Describe the origin and site of ependymal cells.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ependymal cells are ectodermal in origin.
They line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells originate from the ectoderm and line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells are a type of glial cell that arise from the ectoderm, one of the three primary germ layers formed during embryonic development. This ectodermal origin is distinct from other types of glial cells, such as astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, which originate from the neuroectoderm. The unique location of ependymal cells lining the ventricles and central canal allows them to play a crucial role in the production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.text: Describe the shape of ependymal cells.
questions.modelAnswer:
They are cuboidal or columnar cells.
They do not rest on a basement membrane, and their apical surfaces have numerous microvilli and cilia.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells are cuboidal or columnar cells with distinctive apical surface features.
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells are a type of glial cell found in the central nervous system, specifically lining the ventricles and central canal of the spinal cord. They are characterized by their cuboidal or columnar shape, which allows them to form a single layer of cells that can move and circulate cerebrospinal fluid. The presence of numerous microvilli and cilia on their apical surfaces further facilitates this function, enabling the efficient exchange of nutrients and waste products.

questions.text: Classify ependymal cells.
questions.modelAnswer:
They include ependymal cells lining the third and fourth ventricles, tanycytes (ependymal astrocytes), and
choroidal epithelium.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells are a heterogeneous group of cells with distinct subtypes.
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells are a type of glial cell that line the ventricles and central canal of the spinal cord in the central nervous system. They include ependymal cells lining the third and fourth ventricles, tanycytes (ependymal astrocytes), and choroidal epithelium, each with unique morphological and functional characteristics. Understanding the different subtypes of ependymal cells is essential for medical students to appreciate the complex structure and function of the central nervous system.

questions.text: Describe ependymal cells lining the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.modelAnswer:
They are joined by tight junctions and desmosomes.
Their apical surfaces have numerous microvilli.
Numerous mitochondria, basal infoldings, and basal nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells lining the third and fourth ventricles are characterized by their unique ultrastructural features.
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells are specialized cells that line the ventricular system of the brain, including the third and fourth ventricles. They are joined by tight junctions and desmosomes, which provide a tight seal and maintain the integrity of the ventricular system. The apical surfaces of these cells have numerous microvilli, which increase the surface area for the absorption of cerebrospinal fluid, while the presence of numerous mitochondria, basal infoldings, and basal nuclei suggests a high metabolic activity and a role in the production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.text: Mention the functions of ependymal cells.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ependymal cells help circulation of CSF by their cilia and have absorptive function by their microvilli.
Some may be stem cells in the adult human brain, but their neural regenerative potential is still under
investigation.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells play a crucial role in the circulation and absorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells are specialized cells that line the ventricles and central canal of the spinal cord, and they are responsible for the circulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) throughout the central nervous system. The cilia on these cells help to propel CSF, while the microvilli aid in the absorption of CSF, maintaining the delicate balance of fluid within the brain and spinal cord. Additionally, some ependymal cells have been identified as potential stem cells in the adult human brain, although their neural regenerative potential is still being researched.

questions.text: Describe the histological structure of the choroid plexus.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each villus has a central core of pia mater with fenestrated blood capillaries and is covered by columnar
ependymal cells lining the brain ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: The choroid plexus is composed of villi with a central core of pia mater and fenestrated blood capillaries covered by ependymal cells.
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus is a highly specialized structure found in the brain's ventricles, responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The villi of the choroid plexus contain a central core of pia mater, which is surrounded by fenestrated blood capillaries that allow for the exchange of ions and nutrients. The entire structure is lined by columnar ependymal cells, which play a crucial role in the production and secretion of CSF.

questions.text: What is the function of the choroid plexus?
questions.modelAnswer: The choroid plexus secretes cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.keyConcept: The choroid plexus is responsible for the production of cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus, located in the ventricles of the brain, plays a crucial role in the production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). This clear fluid serves as a protective cushion for the brain and spinal cord, providing shock absorption and facilitating the exchange of nutrients and waste products. The choroid plexus secretes CSF through a process involving the active transport of ions and the filtration of blood components, ensuring a stable and healthy environment for the central nervous system.

questions.text: Define hydrocephalus and mention its causes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Hydrocephalus is excess CSF in brain cavities, increasing intracranial pressure.
Causes include decreased absorption of CSF and obstruction of CSF outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Hydrocephalus is characterized by an accumulation of excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the brain's ventricles, leading to increased intracranial pressure.
questions.explanation: This condition occurs when the production or absorption of CSF is disrupted, resulting in a buildup of fluid. The causes of hydrocephalus can be attributed to either decreased absorption of CSF by the arachnoid villi or obstruction of the CSF outflow pathways, such as the aqueduct of Sylvius or the foramina of Magendie and Luschka.

questions.text: List the components of the blood-brain barrier.
questions.modelAnswer:
The BBB is formed of continuous endothelial cells sealed by tight junctions, continuous basement
membrane of endothelial cells, pericytes, and a limiting layer of perivascular astrocytic feet around the
capillary basal lamina.
questions.keyConcept: The blood-brain barrier is a highly selective permeability barrier that separates the circulating blood from the brain and extracellular fluid in the central nervous system.
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier is composed of multiple layers, including continuous endothelial cells sealed by tight junctions, a continuous basement membrane of endothelial cells, pericytes, and a limiting layer of perivascular astrocytic feet around the capillary basal lamina. This complex structure allows for the selective passage of nutrients and ions while restricting the entry of pathogens and toxins into the brain. The integrity of the blood-brain barrier is crucial for maintaining the homeostasis of the central nervous system and preventing neurological disorders.

questions.text: Where is the blood-brain barrier lacking?
questions.modelAnswer:
It is lacking in endocrine regions such as posterior pituitary and pineal body, in regions of the
hypothalamus where plasma components are monitored, and in the choroid plexus where CSF is produced.
questions.keyConcept: The blood-brain barrier is selectively permeable, lacking in certain regions where the exchange of substances between the blood and the brain is necessary.
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier is a highly selective permeable barrier that restricts the passage of certain substances from the blood into the brain. It is lacking in endocrine regions such as the posterior pituitary and pineal body, where the release of hormones into the bloodstream is necessary. Additionally, it is also absent in regions of the hypothalamus where plasma components are monitored and in the choroid plexus, where cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is produced, allowing for the exchange of substances between the blood and the brain in these specific areas.

questions.text: Mention the function of the blood-brain barrier.
questions.modelAnswer:
The BBB protects brain tissue against toxic drugs and harmful substances such as bacteria that may be
present in the blood.
questions.keyConcept: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) functions to protect the brain from harmful substances in the blood.
questions.explanation: The BBB is a highly selective permeability barrier that separates the circulating blood from the brain's extracellular fluid in the central nervous system. It is composed of endothelial cells that are tightly joined together by tight junctions, as well as pericytes and astrocytic end-feet, which further restrict the passage of substances. This selective barrier prevents the entry of toxins, pathogens, and other harmful substances into the brain, maintaining a stable and healthy environment for neuronal function.

questions.text: List the components and function of the blood-CSF barrier.
questions.modelAnswer:
It is formed of endothelial cells of fenestrated capillaries, their basement membrane, connective tissue on
which ependymal cells rest, and ependymal cells connected apically by junctional complexes.
Its function is secretion of CSF.
questions.keyConcept: The blood-CSF barrier is a specialized structure that separates the cerebrospinal fluid from the bloodstream.
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is composed of endothelial cells of fenestrated capillaries, their basement membrane, connective tissue, and ependymal cells. This unique structure allows for the selective passage of substances, while preventing the free exchange of ions and molecules between the blood and CSF. The blood-CSF barrier plays a crucial role in maintaining the homeostasis of the CSF and protecting the central nervous system from external pathogens and toxins.

questions.text: Describe the basic structure of the cerebral cortex.
questions.modelAnswer:
The surface of the cerebrum contains sulci separated by gyri. Gray matter covers gyri and lines sulci and is
formed of nerve cells, neuroglia, and blood capillaries. White matter lies deep to gray matter and is formed
of nerve fibers, neuroglia, and blood capillaries.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebral cortex is composed of distinct layers of gray and white matter.
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex, the outer layer of the cerebrum, is characterized by its convoluted surface, which is divided into sulci and gyri. The gray matter, located on the surface of the gyri and lining the sulci, contains the cell bodies of neurons and supporting glial cells, as well as blood capillaries that supply them with oxygen and nutrients. In contrast, the white matter, situated beneath the gray matter, is composed of myelinated nerve fibers, glial cells, and blood vessels that facilitate the transmission of neural signals.

questions.text: Describe pyramidal cells of the cerebral cortex.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pyramidal cells have pyramidal cell bodies and vary in size from small to giant.
Their apex is directed to the cerebral surface.
